Ionian and Lydian.heading: Hear the scale. Choose its name.
Ionian and Lydian.intro: Listen and choose Ionian or Lydian. The notes go up, then come back down.

steps.title: Listen up and down
steps.description: Press Play and follow the notes as they rise, then return to the starting note. You can listen again whenever you need to.

steps.title: Choose the matching scale
steps.description: Listen for the note that changes between the two choices. Select Ionian or Lydian.

steps.title: Submit your answer
steps.description: When you are ready, press Submit Answer. You can change your choice before you submit.

Ionian and Lydian.about: A scale is a set of notes played in order. Each example rises to a higher version of its starting note, then returns to that starting note. This lesson uses all twelve starting notes. Ionian and Lydian differ at the fourth note. Over C, Ionian uses F and Lydian uses F♯. Listen for that change in the middle of the scale. Choose the scale name. You do not need to enter the notes one by one.
Ionian and Lydian.comparison: Ionian and Lydian differ at the fourth note. Over C, Ionian uses F and Lydian uses F♯. Listen for that change in the middle of the scale.
Ionian and Lydian.exampleExplanation: This visual example shows Ionian starting on C. The notes play one after another, then return down to C. Choose Ionian for this example.

Major Scales #1.about: A scale is a set of notes played in order. Each example rises to a higher version of its starting note, then returns to that starting note. Every example starts and ends on C. This quiz compares the seven modes of the major scale: Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian and Locrian. Their different note patterns give them different sounds. Choose the scale name. You do not need to enter the notes one by one.

Dorian Scales #1.about: A scale is a set of notes played in order. Each example rises to a higher version of its starting note, then returns to that starting note. Every example starts and ends on C. The answers are variants of the same mode family. A few changed notes can change the sound, so listen to the full scale. In the names, ♭ means lowered, ♯ means raised and ♮ means natural. A change of one keyboard step counts both white and black keys. Choose the scale name. You do not need to enter the notes one by one.
Dorian Scales #1.exampleExplanation: This visual example shows Dorian starting on C. The notes play one after another, then return down to C. Choose Dorian for this example.
